name: Cakchiquel
catalog_quote: To distinguish these hypotheses the perception experiment was repeated with speakers of Cakchiquel, a related Mayan language, which has fixed final stress and no phonemic length. ... the final syllable (the normal location of stress) will be longer than any other syllable in the word.

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict' final stress (01 001 0001...) is correct: the Berinstein 1979 quotations are verbatim at pp. vi, 47, 52 of the eScholarship scan (now saved to the audit dir; previously only a /tmp copy existed), and the held 1997 OKMA reference grammar (Rukemik ri Kaqchikel Chi', pp. 20-21, sec. 'Acento') states the same rule explicitly for radical, derived and compound words with directional enclitics attracting the stress, as do the held Bennett 2016 (p.495), Bennett 2018 (fn.7: word-final, no secondary stress) and ALMG 2004, and the newly fetched sources Nelson 2020 acoustic check. No source contradicts. The weakness is only in the pin: the record's deciding citation is a 1979 perception thesis reached through StressTyp2/Gordon 2002, with empty quote/cite/grade fields on the main record, while a native-speaker reference grammar we already hold gives the rule first-hand. Action: re-pin

sources.quote: p. 47: "To distinguish these hypotheses the perception experiment was repeated with speakers of Cakchiquel, a related Mayan language, which has fixed final stress and no phonemic length." Also abstract p. vi: "Both K'ekchi and Cakchiquel have fixed final stress but they differ in that while K'ekchi has phonemic vowel length, Cakchiquel does not." And p. 52: "the final syllable (the normal location of stress) will be longer than any other syllable in the word."

sources.citation: Nelson, Brett C. 2020. Right-Edge Phonological Phenomena in Kaqchikel. Calgary Working Papers in Linguistics 31: 72-88. http://hdl.handle.net/1880/112765
sources.quote: 'The preceding examples show that Kaqchikel does in fact place main word stress on the final syllable of the word. However, there are a few exceptions ... Word-final stress is by far the most common pattern for native vocabulary' -- janila /xanila/ 'very' has penultimate stress (Fig. 6); Spanish loans variable (ruxumprente); 'while Kaqchikel overwhelmingly prefers word-final stress, there is no absolute restriction against other patterns.'
sources.locator: sec. 3.1 'Word stress', pp. 75-77 (acoustic examples, 1-4 syllable words, Figs. 2-7)
sources.note: Only acoustic verification of Kaqchikel word-final stress found (pitch/intensity tracks on 1-4 syllable words); documents the janila and loanword exceptions instrumentally.
